claim: Autonomous coding agents collapse the human-in-the-loop security assumption because the agent acts as both author and reviewer, unlike code-assist tools where a human approves each suggestion.
stance_target: need for adversarial model review / rigid evals (Pillar 1)
quoted_support: Traditional AI security assumes a human is in the loop at critical decision points... Coding agents collapse that assumption, making the agent both author and reviewer.

claim: Coding agents introduce five risk categories traditional security tooling cannot catch: credential/secret exposure, prompt injection through code context, unauthorized tool invocations, unauditable decision chains, and shadow agent proliferation.
stance_target: code blast radius and zero-hallucination quality control architecture (Pillar 1)
quoted_support: The security risks that generative AI introduces go beyond traditional threat models. Coding agents create five distinct categories of risk.

claim: A peer-reviewed arXiv systematic analysis (2601.17548) documents prompt injection vulnerabilities specifically in agentic coding assistants' skills, tools, and protocol ecosystems.
stance_target: security risk of coding-agent context ingestion (Pillar 4/1)
quoted_support: Maloyan, N. and Namiot, D., "Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Coding Assistants: A Systematic Analysis of Vulnerabilities in Skills, Tools, and Protocol Ecosystems," arXiv:2601.17548, 2026.

claim: External LLM-based evaluation at production scale can cost approximately $260,000 annually at 500,000 traces/day, creating an 'AI Trust Tax' that in-environment evaluation models avoid.
stance_target: cost of rigid eval / observability infrastructure at scale (Pillar 6/1)
scope_conditions: directional vendor estimate, varies by model/deployment size/traffic volume
quoted_support: At production scale, enterprises can incur approximately $260K annually at 500K traces per day when using external evaluation. These figures are directional estimates that vary by model, deployment size, and traffic volume.

claim: Enterprises should treat each coding agent as a non-human identity (NHI) in their IAM system, with scoped, rotatable credentials and explicit tool-invocation allowlists.
quoted_support: Treating AI agents as non-human identities with scoped credentials, audit trails, and enforceable policies is the foundation of enterprise agent governance.

claim: Post-execution guardrails on agent-generated outputs (code, commit messages, tool invocations) are a commonly skipped control; teams often only guard user inputs, leaving credential/PII exposure unmitigated on the output side.
quoted_support: A common misconfiguration we see in production is teams deploying AI Guardrails on user inputs but skipping guardrails on agent-generated outputs... Always deploy post-execution guardrails on agent outputs, not just pre-LLM guardrails on inputs.
